_about: The dashboard To-Do feed. Refreshed at every Rule 9 checkpoint alongside the session handoff — this is the handoff distilled into plain language for the 📋 button on every tab. Split For Sam (curation / decisions only a human makes) and For Fable (engineering, the next session picks up).
_status: Dark mode is now correct on most of what a reader actually looks at: the contrast faults the sweep can see fell from 184 to 120, and the light theme did not move once across eight measured passes. The big win was not a color but a counting fix — the report was grouping faults by the HTML element wearing them instead of by the color decision behind them, so the single largest problem (one wrong color, 25 places, 11 tabs) sorted to the bottom of the list looking like twelve small ones. Three separate checks turned out to be incapable of ever reporting a problem, which reads exactly like a clean result: the docs spell-checker was silently switched off below the first indented block in any file, the glyph counter was counting 348 findings that belong to the daily rebuild rather than to us, and it could not see emoji written in escaped form at all — which is how thirteen places telling people to click a padlock button that moved months ago went unnoticed. Those are fixed. What is left for Sam is a judgment call, not a sweep: 26 marks whose removal is a design decision rather than a cleanup, and the banner row, which is not broken and just needs setting.

items.text: Twenty-six glyphs are left and every one is a judgment call rather than a cleanup, so they are yours. The ones that matter: the star on MAP Star Colleges and Veteran Star, where the mark is arguably the name of the designation; the X on close buttons and the pencil on edit; the no-entry mark on blocked gates and the warning triangle on flagged rows. Your rule says a crucial mark stays as a muted CO-blue one — tell me which of these are crucial and I will do the rest. I ask because I swept one of yours this run (the two-way arrow on the crosswalk) and the tests caught it: your own note from July was sitting right there in the code.

The session banner is not broken and never was. The row was switched on but its four-hour window had closed the day before, still pointing at an older session, so the page correctly showed nothing. Setting the session to public does not change this — that decides whether a teammate can OPEN the link, never whether the banner appears. To show it: Admin, Live-session banner, paste the session address, Show the banner. One thing worth deciding: the longest window on offer is eight hours, so a longer working session outlives its own banner with no warning. Say the word and I will add a longer option.

The largest remaining group of dark-mode faults is the same shape repeated with different colors: a panel keeps a pale background that never follows the theme, and the dark text painted over it becomes unreadable. It is the signed-out message, the buttons on Team and RACI, and the activity cards. All of it is measured and named in the lane file, so it is mechanical work with a number to check against.

Seven test files print no readable count of what they checked, so if their checks quietly vanished nothing would notice. The build says so on every run and nobody has claimed it. This is the same failure that hid three real problems this session: a check that cannot fail looks exactly like a check that passed.

The SkyView lane file is two and a half times its size budget and the docs lint says so every run. It is invariants rather than stacked history, so compacting it means reading and ruling on each one — several predate decisions that superseded them. Worth its own sitting rather than another append.

Your ruling on where skill statements come from unblocked the course outline's skills layer — published agency standards are the text of record, an ACE exhibit fills a gap they leave, the MAP team overrides either, and a genuine conflict shows both side by side. But we hold none of that text: of 1,987 credentials classified, 64 of them welding, not one carries a skill field. So this is now a fetching problem, not a decision. The question for you is which published standard to start with — an AWS welding certification is the natural pilot.

You asked for a magic phrase people type before they can move a course, shifting to a team phrase later. That would be the first time anything is written from the map, which today writes nothing at all — so it goes through Governance and the privacy review before it ships rather than after. DR-24 now carries your name as its owner; say the word and the phrase gets scoped.

DR-24 is a governance row with an owner and no surface yet: an added skill lands as proposed with the reviewer's name and the day, and joins the published outline when a second curator agrees; a removal works the same way in reverse. Building that means the map's first write, so it routes through Governance and the privacy review first.

Two housekeeping items behind the CPL face. Fifty-five exhibits in the articulation crosswalk are no longer in today's MAP feed; they stay on the map flagged in words rather than dropped, and the fix is a re-seed of the crosswalk from a fresh custom report. And the credit-funnel numbers the face carries for context were read by hand on 2026-09-07; refresh them after the next custom-report load.
